title: Founding of the Spanish Inquisition
summary: Authorized on November 1, 1478, by Pope Sixtus IV through a papal bull requested by King Ferdinand II and Queen Isabella I, the Spanish Inquisition established a state-controlled ecclesiastical tribunal to detect and punish religious heresy. Initially focusing on Jewish and Muslim converts suspected of secretly practicing their ancestral faiths, the institution became a permanent instrument of crown authority, religious orthodoxy, and severe judicial persecution across Spanish domains.

uncertainty.note: Founding bull dated 1 November 1478 (Julian; Newadvent and Lea agree). End: abolished by decree of the queen regent María Cristina on 15 July 1834 (Britannica). The 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia instead gives 1820 as the definitive abolition; it was abolished in 1808 and 1820 and restored after each, so 1834 is used as the final date.

as_recorded.value: issued a decree abolishing the Spanish Inquisition on July 15, 1834

importance.justification: The Spanish Inquisition created an enduring state-directed apparatus of religious censorship, doctrinal policing, and persecution that defined early modern Spanish governance.

audience_note: Addresses the judicial persecution, torture, and executions directed by the Inquisition against religious minorities, particularly conversos and Moriscos.

reviewer_note: Review 2026-11-12: founding date, Seville tribunal (1480) and crown control checked against Newadvent and Lea. The 1834 end date was unsourced and the Catholic Encyclopedia says 1820; Britannica added for 1834 and the disagreement noted. Pin is Seville, where the first tribunal sat; the bull itself was issued in Rome.
